extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and parties practicing before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB); trademark litigants and counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural standards for discovery remedies, sanctions, depositions, requests for admission, and the Board’s standard and modified protective orders in TTAB inter partes proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to compel before sanctions for disclosure failures
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to compel is the available remedy when an adversary has failed to make, or has made inadequate, initial disclosures or disclosures of expert testimony; a motion to compel must precede a motion for sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Cites: 37 CFR § 2.120(e); Misc. Changes to TTAB Rules, 72 Fed. Reg. 42242 (Aug. 1, 2007); cases such as Luster Products Inc. v. Van Zandt and Influance v. Zuker). See TBMP § 527.01 for further information concerning discovery sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of motion to compel for initial disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to compel for failure to serve initial disclosures is to be filed prior to the close of the discovery period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Cites: 37 CFR § 2.120(e); Luster Products Inc. v. Van Zandt, 104 USPQ2d 1877 (TTAB 2012)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions under 37 CFR § 2.120(g) only after motion to compel granted
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion for sanctions under 37 CFR § 2.120(g)(1) is only appropriate if a motion to compel the respective disclosures has already been granted; motions for sanctions may be denied as premature if no Board order compelling discovery is in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Cites: Misc. Changes to TTAB Rules; Amazon Technologies v. Wax; see also discussion of 37 CFR § 2.120(g)(2) and Kairos Institute v. Doolittle Gardens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling interrogatory answers and document production
rubrics_metrics.description: If any party fails to answer any interrogatory or fails to produce and permit inspection and copying of any document or thing, the party seeking discovery may file a motion with the Board for an order to compel an answer or production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The party seeking interrogatory responses or production may not seek immediate entry of sanctions for no response unless the responding party has expressly informed the inquiring party that no response will be made to the discovery requests. For motions to compel, see TBMP § 523. (Cites: 37 CFR § 2.120(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for admission — consequences of failure to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party served with requests for admission fails to file a timely response, the requests will stand admitted unless the failure was the result of excusable neglect or unless a motion to withdraw or amend the admissions is filed pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 36(b) and granted by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See TBMP § 407.03(a) for time to serve responses and TBMP § 525 for motions to withdraw/amend admissions. (Cites: Fed. R. Civ. P. 36; 37 CFR § 2.120(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to determine sufficiency of admissions responses
rubrics_metrics.description: If dissatisfied with an answer or objection to a request for admission, the propounding party may file a motion with the Board to determine the sufficiency of the response or objection; the Board may order the matter admitted, an amended answer, or that a response be served if an objection is unjustified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a request is admitted or denied, such admissions or denials constitute a proper response even if the response also includes objections; the requesting party should refrain from challenging the sufficiency of such a response. (See TBMP § 524).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) designations and deposition attendance/answers
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party fails to designate a person under Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) or 31(a)(4), or a designated person or party officer fails to attend or answer at a discovery deposition, the party seeking discovery may file a motion to compel designation, attendance, or an answer with the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board does not have jurisdiction over non-party witnesses; enforcement of subpoenas for non-party witnesses must be sought in the issuing federal district court. If a deponent objects at a deposition, the question normally should be answered subject to the stated objection. If a deponent refuses to answer at a deposition taken pursuant to a subpoena, the propounding party may seek immediate relief from the federal district court under 35 U.S.C. § 24; absent a court order, the propounding party may complete the deposition and then seek relief from the Board. (Cites: 37 CFR § 2.120(e); Neville Chemical Co. v. Lubrizol Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board’s range of sanctions for discovery misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: For failure to provide disclosures or discovery, the Board may impose a variety of sanctions rooted in Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(b)(2), including striking pleadings, refusing to allow support or opposition of claims/defenses, drawing adverse inferences, prohibiting introduction of designated matters, and entering judgment against the disobedient party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will not hold any person in contempt or award expenses, including attorneys' fees, to any party. See TBMP § 527.01 for further information. (Cites: Fed. R. Civ. P. 37; 37 CFR § 2.116).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic application of Board’s standard protective order
rubrics_metrics.description: For inter partes proceedings pending or commenced on or after August 31, 2007, the Board’s standard protective order is automatically in place to govern the exchange of information unless the parties, by stipulation approved by the Board, agree to an alternative order, or a motion to use an alternative order is granted by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board’s notice of institution will advise parties that the standard protective order applies; the standard protective order is available on the USPTO website. Parties need not sign it for effect but may do so. Cases commenced prior to Aug. 31, 2007 with approved protective orders are not affected. (Cites: 37 CFR § 2.116(g); Misc. Changes to TTAB Rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three tiers of protected information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board’s standard protective order provides for three tiers of protected information: (1) Confidential; (2) Highly Confidential; and (3) Trade Secret/Commercially Sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties and their attorneys shall have access to Confidential and Highly Confidential materials (subject to agreed exceptions). Outside counsel, but not in-house counsel, shall have access to Trade Secret/Commercially Sensitive materials. Parties and pro se individuals will not have access to Trade Secret material. Independent experts/consultants and non-party witnesses may be afforded access in accordance with the order and must sign acknowledgements. The Board may sanction breaches. (See TBMP § 412.01 and notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information not eligible for protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Information may not be designated as subject to protection if it: (a) is or becomes public knowledge (other than through violation of the order); (b) is acquired by a non-designating party or non-party witness from a third party lawfully possessing the information; (c) was lawfully possessed prior to discovery with written evidence; (d) is disclosed by a non-designating party legally compelled to disclose; or (e) is disclosed by a non-designating party with approval of the designating party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exclusions prevent overbroad or improper designation of confidentiality under the protective order. (See TBMP § 412, Excerpts from Standard Protective Order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Access rules and definitions for persons covered by protective order
rubrics_metrics.description: The protective order defines who constitutes parties, attorneys (including in-house counsel and support staff), independent experts/consultants, and non-party witnesses and sets who may access protected information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges, attorneys, and Board employees are bound to honor designations but are not required to sign acknowledgement forms; court reporters and technicians are bound only to the extent the parties condition employment or obtain agreements. (See TBMP § 412 Excerpts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on party seeking protection and waiver by failure to designate
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden falls on the party seeking to designate information as protected; parties must actively utilize the provisions when seeking protection. If a party fails to designate or redact confidential portions, confidentiality is deemed waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The designating party has a duty to make a meaningful effort to designate only information that warrants the protection level; excessive markings often indicate improper designation and may lead to redesignation or a show cause order. (Cites: Wet Seal, Inc. v. FD Management, Inc.; General Mills v. Fage). See TBMP § 412.01 and § 703.01(p) for redaction procedures at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality is not a basis to withhold properly discoverable information
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties cannot withhold properly discoverable information on the basis of confidentiality since the Board’s standard protective order automatically applies; the Board may order production consistent with the terms of the protective order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a party refuses to provide discoverable information on confidentiality grounds, the Board may require production under the protective order. (Cites: 37 CFR § 2.120(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties may modify the standard protective order by stipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are free to modify the terms of the Board’s standard protective order and are encouraged to discuss proposed modifications during the discovery conference; stipulated protective orders should be filed with the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An executed stipulated protective order should be filed with the Board; parties should not wait for acknowledgement to act per the agreement. Modifications cannot be used to circumvent 37 CFR § 2.27(d) and (e) regarding public inspection of files. (See TBMP § 412.02(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective orders under 37 CFR § 2.120(f) and the good-cause standard
rubrics_metrics.description: On motion and for good cause, the Board may make any order justice requires to protect a party from annoyance, embarrassment, oppression, or undue burden or expense, including types of orders listed in Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c)(A)–(H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish good cause, the movant must submit a particular and specific demonstration of fact, not stereotyped or conclusory statements; the movant bears the burden of showing good cause and that its ability to litigate will be prejudiced (not merely made more difficult). (Cites: 37 CFR § 2.120(f); Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c); cases such as FMR Corp. v. Alliant Partners and A. Hirsh v. U.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification of protective order for pro se litigants and in-house counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard protective order disallows access to trade secret/commercially sensitive information by pro se litigants and in-house counsel absent modification; financial burden is not good cause to permit access for these individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in-house counsel seeks access to trade secret material, the key factor is whether the in-house counsel is involved in the employer-litigant's competitive decision-making. Courts and the Board apply a competitive decision-making test. (Cites: A. Hirsh, Inc. v. United States; U.S. Steel Corp. v. United States; Georgia Pacific v. Solo Cup).

rubrics_metrics.name: In camera inspection to resolve relevance/confidentiality disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Board cannot determine from party arguments whether a document is relevant/confidential on a motion to compel, it may request submission of the document for in camera inspection and then return it to the submitting party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In camera inspection has been used to validate trade secret designations. (Cites: Amazon Technologies, Inc. v. Wax). See TBMP § 412.02(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical contents and provisions of a modified protective order
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised protective orders typically clarify: definitions of confidential/trade secret material; handling procedures; requirement to designate prior to disclosure; reasonable_basis requirement for designations; exclusions for previously known/independently developed/public/third-party-acquired information; specification of persons with access; notice to recipients of terms; limitation of use to the proceeding; dispute-resolution means; filing procedures for confidential submissions and requirement for confidential and redacted versions; return/destroy obligations at termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific provisions listed (1)–(13) in TBMP § 412.02(d) include ESTTA electronic filing instructions (CONFIDENTIAL designation), filing two versions (confidential and redacted), and preference for ESTTA. For additional case law guidance see cited authorities (e.g., Johnston Pump; Neville Chemical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing and recordation of confidential materials
rubrics_metrics.description: To make confidential or trade secret material part of the record, it must be submitted electronically designated as “CONFIDENTIAL” in ESTTA, or by paper in a separate sealed envelope marked “CONFIDENTIAL.” Confidential submissions require two versions — a confidential version and a redacted version available for public viewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are encouraged to file confidential and trade secret materials through ESTTA; see TBMP §§ 120.02, 412.04, and 412.05 for filing details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and post-termination handling of protected materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board’s jurisdiction ends when the proceeding is terminated (final order and appeals resolved or appeal period lapsed); within 30 days after final termination, parties and their attorneys shall return to each disclosing party all protected information or, alternatively, the disclosing party may request destruction of the materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board's protective order leaves uncertain whether the Board can order post-termination contractual obligations; parties and attorneys may wish to sign a stipulated protective order to create contractual rights enforceable in court after the proceeding. (See TBMP § 412.03 and notes).
